entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.26.1-Job.4.1">Job 26:1-4  1</reference>  Then Job began, and said:  2  How has thou helped him that is without power, <div eID="gen7977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> Raised the arm that hath no strength!   3  How hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom, <div eID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7979" type="x-p"/> And fully declared the essence of the matter!   4  To whom hast thou uttered words, <div eID="gen7979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> And whose breath proceeded from thee? <div eID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7981" type="x-p"/> Bildad is the person addressed, and the exclamations in <reference osisRef="Job.26.2">Job 26:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.26.3">Job 26:3</reference> are ironical: how thy speech contains nothing whatever that might help me, the supposedly feeble one, in conquering my affliction and my temptation; me, the supposedly ignorant one, in comprehending man’s mysterious lot, and mine! ללא־כח, according to the idea, is only equivalent to כח לו (אין) לאשׁר לא, and זרוע לא־עז equivalent to זרוע בלא־עז (לא עז לו); the former is the <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concreto,</hi> the latter the genitival connection - the arm of the no-power, i.e., powerless (Ges. §152, 1). The powerless one is Job himself, not God (Merc., Schlottm.), as even the choice of the verbs, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.2">Job 26:2</reference></hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.3">Job 26:3</reference></hi>, shows. Respecting תּוּשׁיּה, which we have translated essentiality, duration, completion, we said, on <reference osisRef="Job.5.12">Job 5:12</reference>, that it is formed from ישׁ (vid., <reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Pro 8:21</reference>), not directly indeed, but by means of a verb ושׁי brev a fo  (ושׁה), in the signification subsistere (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">kân</hi>, and Syriac קום);<note placement="foot">Comp. also Spiegel, <hi type="italic">Grammatik der Huzväresch-Sprache,</hi> S. 103.</note> it is a <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi>-formation (like תּוּגה), and signifies, so to speak, durability, <hi type="italic">subsistentia, substantia,</hi> ὑπόστασις, so that the comparison of ושׁי with אשׁשׁ, Arab. <hi type="italic">'ss</hi> (whence אשׁישׁ, Arab. <hi type="italic">ası̂s , asâs ,</hi> etc., <hi type="italic">fundamentum</hi>) is forced upon one, and the relationship to the Sanskrit <hi type="italic">as</hi> (<hi type="italic">asmi</hi> = εἰμὶ) can remain undecided. The observation of J. D. Michaelis<note placement="foot">Against the comparison of the Arab. <hi type="italic">wâsâ , solari,</hi> by Michaelis, Ges., and others (who assume the primary significations <hi type="italic">solatium, auxilium</hi>), Lagarde (<hi type="italic">Anmerkungen zur griech. Uebersetzung der Proverbien,</hi> 1863, S. 57f.) correctly remarks that Arab. <hi type="italic">wâsâ ,</hi> is only a change of letters of the common language for Arab. <hi type="italic">âsâ ;</hi> but Arab. <hi type="italic">wâšâ</hi>, to finish painting (whence Arab. <hi type="italic">twšyt</hi>, decoration), or ושׁה as a transposition from שׁוה, to be level, simple (Hitzig on <reference osisRef="Prov.3.21">Pro 3:21</reference>), leads to no suitable sense.</note> to the contrary, <hi type="italic">Supplem</hi>. p. 1167: <hi type="italic">non placent in linguis ejusmodi etyma metaphysica nimis a vulgari sensu remota; philosophi in scholis ejusmodi vocabula condunt, non plebs,</hi> is removed by the consideration that תושׁיה, which out of Prov. and Job occurs only in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.29">Isa 28:29</reference>, Mich. <reference osisRef="Job.6.9">Job 6:9</reference>, is a Chokma-word: it signifies here, as frequently, <hi type="italic">vera et realis sapientia</hi> (J. H. Michaelis). The speech of Bildad is a proof of poverty of thought, of which he himself gives the evidence. His words - such is the thought of <reference osisRef="Job.26.4">Job 26:4</reference> - are altogether inappropriate, inasmuch as they have no reference whatever to the chief point of Job’s speech; and they are, moreover, not his own, but the suggestion of another, and that not God, but Eliphaz, from whom Bildad has borrowed the substance of his brief declamation. Since this is the meaning of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.4">Job 26:4</reference></hi>, it might seem as though את־מי were intended to signify by whose assistance (Arnh., Hahn); but as the poet also, in <reference osisRef="Job.31.37">Job 31:37</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.10">Eze 43:10</reference>, uses הגּיד <hi type="italic">seq. acc.,</hi> in the sense of explaining anything to any one, to instruct him concerning anything, it is to be interpreted: to whom hast thou divulged the words (lxx, τίνι ἀνήγγειλας ῥήματα), i.e., thinking and designing thereby to affect him? <div eID="gen7981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7982" type="x-p"/> In what follows, Job now continues the description of God’s exalted rule, which Bildad had attempted, by tracing it through every department of creation; and thus proves by fact, that he is wanting neither in a recognition nor reverence of God the almighty Ruler.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.26.5-Job.7.5">Job 26:5-7   5</reference>   - The shades are put to pain <div eID="gen7982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7983" type="x-p"/> Deep under the waters and their inhabitants.   6  Sheôl is naked before him, <div eID="gen7983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7984" type="x-p"/> And the abyss hath no covering.   7  He stretched the northern sky over the emptiness; <div eID="gen7984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7985" type="x-p"/> He hung the earth upon nothing. <div eID="gen7985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7986" type="x-p"/> Bildad has extolled God’s majestic, awe-inspiring rule in the heights of heaven, His immediate surrounding; Job continues the strain, and celebrates the extension of this rule, even to the depths of the lower world. The operation of the majesty of the heavenly Ruler extends even to the realm of shades; the sea with the multitude of its inhabitants forms no barrier between God and the realm of shades; the marrowless, bloodless phantoms or shades below writhe like a woman in travail as often as this majesty is felt by them, as, perhaps, by the raging of the sea or the quaking of the earth. On רפאים, which also occurs in Phoenician inscriptions, vid., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 409; the book of Job corresponds with <reference osisRef="Ps.88.11">Psa 88:11</reference> in the use of this appellation. The <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. is not רפאי (whence רפאים, as the name of a people), but רפא (רפה), which signifies both giants or heroes of colossal stature (from רפה = Arab. <hi type="italic">rafu‛a ,</hi> to be high), and the relaxed (from רפה, to be loose, like Arab. <hi type="italic">rafa'a ,</hi> to soften, to soothe), i.e., those who are bodiless in the state after death (comp. חלּה, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.10">Isa 14:10</reference>, to be weakened, i.e., placed in the condition of a <hi type="italic">rapha</hi>). It is a question whether יחוללוּ be <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> (Ges.) or <hi type="italic">Pulal</hi> (Olsh.); the <hi type="italic">Pul.,</hi> indeed, signifies elsewhere to be brought forth with writing (<reference osisRef="Job.15.7">Job 15:7</reference>); it can, however, just as well signify to be put in pain. On account of the reference implied in it to a higher causation here at the commencement of the speech, the <hi type="italic">Pul</hi>. is more appropriate than the <hi type="italic">Pil.;</hi> and the pausal <hi type="italic">â</hi>, which is often found elsewhere with <hi type="italic">Hithpael</hi> (<hi type="italic">Hithpal</hi>.), <reference osisRef="Ps.88.14">Psa 88:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.5">Job 33:5</reference>, but never with <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> (<hi type="italic">Pil</hi>.), proves that the form is intended to be regarded as passive.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.26.8-Job.10.8">Job 26:8-10   8</reference>  He bindeth up the waters in His clouds, <div eID="gen7987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7988" type="x-p"/> Without the clouds being rent under their burden.   9  He enshroudeth the face of His throne, <div eID="gen7988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7989" type="x-p"/> Spreading His clouds upon it. 10  He compasseth the face of the waters with bounds, <div eID="gen7989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7990" type="x-p"/> To the boundary between light and darkness. <div eID="gen7990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7991" type="x-p"/> The clouds consist of masses of water rolled together, which, if they were suddenly set free, would deluge the ground; but the omnipotence of God holds the waters together in the hollow of the clouds (צרר, <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, according to a recognised law, although it is also found in Codd. accented as <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, but contrary to the Masora), so that they do not burst asunder under the burden of the waters (תּחתּם); by which nothing more nor less is meant, than that the physical and meteorological laws of rain are of God’s appointment. <reference osisRef="Job.26.9">Job 26:9</reference> describes the dark and thickly-clouded sky that showers down the rain in the appointed rainy season. אחז signifies to take hold of, in architecture to hold together by means of beams, or to fasten together (vid., Thenius on 1Ki 6:10, comp. <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.18">2Ch 9:18</reference>, מאחזים, <hi type="italic">coagmentata</hi>), then also, as usually in Chald. and Syr., to shut (by means of cross-bars, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.3">Neh 7:3</reference>), here to shut off by surrounding with clouds: He shuts off פּני־כסּה, the front of God’s throne, which is turned towards the earth, so that it is hidden by storm-clouds as by a סכּה, <reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference>; Psa 18:12. God’s throne, which is here, as in 1Ki 10:19, written כּסּה instead of כּסּא (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">cursi</hi>, of the throne of God the Judge, in distinction from Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ‛arš ,</hi> the throne of God who rules over the world),<note placement="foot">According to the more recent interpretation, under Aristotelian influence, Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ‛rš</hi> is the outermost sphere, which God as πρῶτον κινοῦν having set in motion, communicates light, heat, life, and motion to the other revolving spheres; for the <hi type="italic">causae mediae</hi> gradually descend from God the Author of being (<hi type="italic">muhejji</hi>) from the highest heaven into the sublunary world.</note> is indeed in other respects invisible, but the cloudless blue of heaven is His reflected splendour (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.10">Exo 24:10</reference>) which is cast over the earth. God veils this His radiance which shines forth towards the earth, פּרשׁז אליו עננו, by spreading over it the clouds which are led forth by Him. פּרשׁו is commonly regarded as a Chaldaism for פּרשׁז (Ges. §56, Olsh. §276), but without any similar instance in favour of this vocalizaton of the 3 <hi type="italic">pr. Piel</hi> (<hi type="italic">Pil</hi>.). Although רענן and שׁאנן, <reference osisRef="Job.15.32">Job 15:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.3.18">Job 3:18</reference>, have given up the <hi type="italic">i</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Pil.,</hi> it has been under the influence of the following guttural; and although, moreover, <hi type="italic">i</hi> before <hi type="italic">Resh</hi> sometimes passes into <hi type="italic">a</hi>, e.g., ויּרא, it is more reliable to regard פרשז as <hi type="italic">inf. absol</hi>. (Ew. §141, <hi type="italic">c</hi>): <hi type="italic">expandendo</hi>. Ges. and others regard this פרשז as a mixed form, composed from פרשׁ and פרז; but the verb פרשׁ (with <hi type="italic">Shin</hi>) has not the signification to expand, which is assumed in connection with this derivation; it signifies to separate (also <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12">Eze 34:12</reference>, vid., Hitzig on that passage), whereas פרשׂ certainly signifies to expand (<reference osisRef="Job.36.29-Job.36.30">Job 36:29-30</reference>); wherefore the reading פּרשׂז (with <hi type="italic">Sin</hi>), which some Codd. give, is preferred by Bär, and in agreement with him by Luzzatto (vid., Bär’s <hi type="italic">Leket zebi,</hi> p. 244), and it seems to underlie the interpretation where פרשז עליו is translated by עליו (פּרשׂ) פרש, He spreadeth over it (e.g., by Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, Ralbag). But the Talmud, <hi type="italic">b. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.26.11-Job.13.11">Job 26:11-13 11</reference>  The pillars of heaven tremble <div eID="gen7992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7993" type="x-p"/> And are astonished at His threatening. 12  By His power He rouseth up the sea, <div eID="gen7993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7994" type="x-p"/> And by His understanding He breaketh Rahab in pieces. 13  By His breath the heavens become cheerful; <div eID="gen7994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7995" type="x-p"/> His hand hath formed the fugitive dragon. <div eID="gen7995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7996" type="x-p"/> The mountains towering up to the sky, which seem to support the vault of the sky, are called poetically “the pillars of heaven.” ירופפוּ is <hi type="italic">Pulal</hi>, like יחוללוּ, <reference osisRef="Job.26.5">Job 26:5</reference>; the signification of violent and quick motion backwards and forwards is secured to the verb רוּף by the Targ. אתרופף = התפּלּץ, <reference osisRef="Job.9.6">Job 9:6</reference>, and the Talm. רפרף of churned milk, blinding eyes (comp. הרף עין, the twinkling of the eye, and Arab. <hi type="italic">rff , fut. i. o. nictare</hi>), flapping wings (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">rff</hi> and <hi type="italic">rfrf , movere, motitare alas</hi>), of wavering thinking. גּערה is the divine command which looses or binds the powers of nature; the astonishment of the supports of heaven is, according to the radical signification of תּמהּ (cogn. שׁמם), to be conceived of as a torpidity which follows the divine impulse, without offering any resistance whatever. That רגע, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.12">Job 26:12</reference></hi>, is to be understood transitively, not like <reference osisRef="Job.7.5">Job 7:5</reference>, intransitively, is proved by the dependent (borrowed) passages, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.15">Isa 51:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.35">Jer 31:35</reference>, from which it is also evident that רגע cannot with the lxx be translated κατέπαυσεν. The verb combines in itself the opposite significations of starting up, i.e., entering into an excited state, and of being startled, from which the significations of stilling (<hi type="italic">Niph., Hiph.</hi>), and of standing back or retreat (Arab. <hi type="italic">rj‛</hi>), branch off. The conjecture גּער after the Syriac version (which translates, <hi type="italic">go‛ar bejamo</hi>) is superfluous. רהב, which here also is translated by the lxx τὸ κῆτος, has been discussed already on Job 9:13. It is not meant of the turbulence of the sea, to which מחץ is not appropriate, but of a sea monster, which, like the crocodile and the dragon, are become an emblem of Pharaoh and his power, as Isa 51:9. has applied this primary passage: the writer of the book of Job purposely abstains from such references to the history of Israel. Without doubt, רהב denotes a demoniacal monster, like the demons that shall be destroyed at the end of the world, one of which is called by the Persians <hi type="italic">akomano</hi>, evil thought, another <hi type="italic">taromaiti</hi>, pride. This view is supported by <reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference>, where one is not at liberty to determine the meaning by <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>, and to understand נחשׁ בּרח, like תּנּין in that passage, of Egypt. But this dependent passage is an important indication for the correct rendering of חללה. One thing is certain at the outset, that שׁפרה is not <hi type="italic">perf. Piel</hi> = שׁפרה, and for this reason, that the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> which characterizes <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> cannot be omitted from any of the six <hi type="italic">mutae;</hi> the translation of Jerome, <hi type="italic">spiritus ejus ornavit coelos,</hi> and all similar ones, are therefore false. But it is possible to translate: “by His spirit (creative spirit) the heavens are beauty, His hand has <hi type="italic">formed</hi> the flying dragon.” Thus, in the signification to bring forth (as <reference osisRef="Prov.25.23">Pro 25:23</reference>; Pro 8:24.), חללה is rendered by Rosenm., Arnh., Vaih., Welte, Renan, and others, of whom Vaih. and Renan, however, do not understand <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference></hi> of the creation of the heavens, but of their illumination. By this rendering <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference></hi> are severed, as being without connection; in general, however, the course of thought in the description does not favour the reference of the whole of half of <reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference> to the creation. Accordingly, חללה is not to be taken as <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> from חול (ליל), but after <reference osisRef="Isa.57.9">Isa 57:9</reference>, as <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> from חלל, according to which the idea of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference></hi> is determined, since both lines of the verse are most closely connected. (בּריח) נחשׁ בּרח is, to wit, the constellation of the Dragon,<note placement="foot">Ralbag, without any ground for it, understands it of the milky way (העגול החלבי), which, according to Rapoport, Pref. to Slonimski’s <hi type="italic">Toledoth ha-schamajim</hi> (1838), was already known to the Talmud <hi type="italic">b. Berachoth</hi>, 58 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, under the name of נהר דנוד.</note> one of the most straggling constellations, which winds itself between the Greater and Lesser Bears almost half through the polar circle. <div eID="gen7996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7997" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Maximus hic plexu sinuoso elabitur Anguis Circum perque duas in morem fluminis Arctos</hi>.” (Virgil, Georg. i. 244f.) <div eID="gen7997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7998" type="x-p"/> Aratus in Cicero, <hi type="italic">de nat. Deorum,</hi> ii. 42, describes it more graphically, both in general, and in regard to the many stars of different magnitudes which form its body from head to tail. Among the Arabs it is called <hi type="italic">el - hajje ,</hi> the serpent, e.g., in Firuzabâdi: the <hi type="italic">hajje</hi> is a constellation between the Lesser Bear (<hi type="italic">farqadân</hi>, the two calves) and the Greater Bear (<hi type="italic">benât en - na‛sch ,</hi> the daughters of the bier), “or <hi type="italic">et - tanı̂n ,</hi> the dragon, e.g., in one of the authors quoted by Hyde on Ulugh Beigh’s <hi type="italic">Tables of the Stars,</hi> p. 18: the tanîn lies round about the north pole in the form of a long serpent, with many bends and windings.” Thus far the testimony of the old expositors is found in Rosenmüller. The Hebrew name תּלי (the quiver) is perhaps to be distinguished from טלי and דּלי, the Zodiac constellations Aries and Aquarius.<note placement="foot">Vid., <hi type="italic">Wissenschaft, Kunst, Judenthum</hi> (1838), S. 220f.</note> <div eID="gen7998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7999" type="x-p"/> It is questionable how בּרח is to be understood. The lxx translates δράκοντα ἀποστάτην in this passage, which is certainly incorrect, since בריח beside נחשׁ may naturally be assumed to be an attributive word referring to the motion or form of the serpent. Accordingly, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>, ὄφιν φείγοντα is more correct, where the Syr. version is חויא חרמנא, the fierce serpent, which is devoid of support in the language; in the passage before us the Syr. also has חויא דערק, the fleeing serpent, but this translation does not satisfy the more neuter signification of the adjective. Aquila in Isaiah translates ὄφιν μόχλον, as Jerome translates the same passage <hi type="italic">serpentem vectem</hi> (whereas he translates <hi type="italic">coluber tortuosus</hi> in our passage), as though it were בּריח; Symm. is better, and without doubt a substantially similar thought, ὄφιν συγκλείοντα, the serpent that joins by a bolt, which agrees with the traditional Jewish explanation, for the dragon in Aben-Ezra and Kimchi (in <hi type="italic">Lex.</hi>) - after the example of the learned Babylonian teacher of astronomy, Mar-Samuel (died 257), who says of himself that the paths of the heavens are as familiar to him as the places of Nehardea<note placement="foot">Vid., Grätz, <hi type="italic">Geschichte der Juden,</hi> iv. 324. On <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference> Kimchi interprets the מבריח differently: he scares (pushes away).</note>  - is called נחשׁ עקלתון, because it is as though it were wounded, and בריח, because it forms a bar (מבריח) from one end of the sky to the other; or as Sabbatai Donolo (about 94), the Italian astronomer,<note placement="foot">Vid., extracts from his המזלות ספר in Joseph Kara’s <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job,</hi> contributed by S. D. Luzzatto in <hi type="italic">Kerem Chemed,</hi> 7th year, S. 57ff.</note> expresses it: “When God created the two lights (the sun and moon) and the five stars (planets) and the twelve מזלור (the constellations of the Zodiac), He also created the תלי (dragon), to unite these heavenly bodies as by a weaver’s beam (מנור אורגים), and made it stretch itself on the firmament from one end to another as a bar (כבריח), like a wounded serpent furnished with the head and tail.” By this explanation בּריח is either taken directly as בּריח, <hi type="italic">vectis</hi>, in which signification it does not, however, occur elsewhere, or the signification <hi type="italic">transversus</hi> (<hi type="italic">transversarius</hi>) is assigned to the בּריח (= <hi type="italic">barrı̂ah</hi>) with an unchangeable <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi>, - a signification which it might have, for brch Arab. <hi type="italic">brḥ</hi> signifies properly to go through, to go slanting across, of which the meanings to unite slanting and to slip away are only variations. בּריח, notwithstanding, has in the language, so far as it is preserved to us, everywhere the signification <hi type="italic">fugitivus</hi>, and we will also keep to this: the dragon in the heavens is so called, as having the appearance of fleeing and hastening away. But in what sense is it said of God, that He pierces or slays it? The mountains towering up to the sky, which seem to support the vault of the sky, are called poetically “the pillars of heaven.” ירופפוּ is Pulal , like יחוללוּ, Job 26:5 ; the signification of violent and quick motion backwards and forwards is secured to the verb רוּף by the Targ. אתרופף = התפּלּץ, Job 9:6 , and the Talm. רפרף of churned milk, blinding eyes (comp. הרף עין, the twinkling of the eye, and Arab. rff , fut. i. o. nictare ), flapping wings (comp. Arab. rff and rfrf , movere, motitare alas ), of wavering thinking. גּערה is the divine command which looses or binds the powers of nature; the astonishment of the supports of heaven is, according to the radical signification of תּמהּ (cogn. שׁמם), to be conceived of as a torpidity which follows the divine impulse, without offering any resistance whatever. That רגע, Job 26:12 , is to be understood transitively, not like Job 7:5 , intransitively, is proved by the dependent (borrowed) passages, Isa 51:15 ; Jer 31:35 , from which it is also evident that רגע cannot with the lxx be translated κατέπαυσεν. The verb combines in itself the opposite significations of starting up, i.e., entering into an excited state, and of being startled, from which the significations of stilling ( Niph., Hiph. ), and of standing back or retreat (Arab. rj‛ ), branch off. Without doubt, רהב denotes a demoniacal monster, like the demons that shall be destroyed at the end of the world, one of which is called by the Persians akomano , evil thought, another taromaiti , pride. Piel = שׁפרה, and for this reason, that the Dagesh which characterizes Piel cannot be omitted from any of the six mutae; the translation of Jerome, spiritus ejus ornavit coelos, and all similar ones, are therefore false. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">Job 26:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">14</reference>  Behold, these are the edges of His ways, <div eID="gen8000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8001" type="x-p"/> And how do we hear only a whisper thereof! <div eID="gen8001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8002" type="x-p"/> But the thunder of His might - who comprehendeth it? <div eID="gen8002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8003" type="x-p"/> These (אלּה retrospective, as in <reference osisRef="Job.18.21">Job 18:21</reference>) are only קצות, the extremest end-points or outlines of the ways of God, which Job has depicted; the wondrous fulness of His might, which extends through the whole creation, transcends human comprehension; it is only שׁמץ דּבר therefrom that becomes audible to us men. שׁמץ (שׁמץ) is translated by Symm. here ψιθύρισμα, <reference osisRef="Job.4.12">Job 4:12</reference>, ψιτηυρισμός; the Arab. <hi type="italic">šamiṣa</hi> (to speak very quickly, mutter) confirms this idea of the word; Jerome’s translation, <hi type="italic">vix. parvam stillam sermonis ejus </hi>(comp. <reference osisRef="Job.4.12">Job 4:12</reference>, <hi type="italic">venas</hi>, tropical for parts), is doubly erroneous: the rendering of the שׁמץ has the antithesis of רעם against it, and דּבר is not to be understood here otherwise than in ערות דּבר, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.15">Deu 23:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.1">Deu 24:1</reference> : shame of something = something that excites a feeling of shame, a whisper of something = some whisper. The notion “somewhat,” which the old expositors attribute to שׁמץ, lies therefore in דבר. מה is exclamatory in a similar manner as in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.48">Psa 89:48</reference> : how we hear (נשׁמע, not נשׁמע) only some whisper thereof (בּו partitive, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference>), i.e., how little therefrom is audible to us, only as the murmur of a word, not loud and distinct, which reaches us! <div eID="gen8003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8004" type="x-p"/> As in the speech of Bildad the poet makes the opposition of the friends to fade away and cease altogether, as incapable of any further counsel, and hence as conquered, so in Job’s closing speech, which consists of three parts, <reference osisRef="Job.26.1">Job 26:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.27.1">Job 27:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.1">Job 29:1</reference>, he shows how Job in every respect, as victor, maintains the field against the friends. The friends have neither been able to loose the knot of Job’s lot of suffering, nor the universal distribution of prosperity and misfortune. Instead of loosing the knot of Job’s lot of suffering, they have cut it, by adding to Job’s heavy affliction the invention of heinous guilt as its ground of explanation; and the knot of the contradictions of human life in general with divine justice they have ignored, in order that they may not be compelled to abandon their dogma, that suffering everywhere necessarily presupposes sin, and sin is everywhere necessarily followed by suffering. Even Job, indeed, is not at present able to solve either one or other of the mysteries; but while the friends’ treatment of these mysteries is untrue, he honours the truth, and keenly perceives that which is mysterious. Then he proves by testimony and an appeal to facts, that the mystery may be acknowledged without therefore being compelled to abandon the fear of God. Job firmly holds to the objective reality and the testimony of his consciousness; in the fear of God he places himself above all those contradictions which are unsolvable by and perplexing to human reason; his faith triumphs over the rationalism of the friends, which is devoid of truth, of justice, and of love. <div eID="gen8004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8005" type="x-p"/> Job first answers Bildad, Job 26:1. He characterizes his poor reply as what it is: as useless, and not pertinent in regard to the questions before them: it is of no service to him, it does not affect him, and is, moreover, a borrowed weapon. For he also is conscious of and can praise God’s exalted and awe-inspiring majesty. He has already shown this twice, <reference osisRef="Job.9.4-Job.9.10">Job 9:4-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.13-Job.12.25">Job 12:13-25</reference>, and shows here for the third time: its operation is not confined merely to those creatures that immediately surround God in the heavens; it extends, without being restrained by the sea, even down to the lower world; and as it makes the angels above to tremble, so there it sets the shades in consternation. From the lower world, Job’s contemplation rises to the earth, as a body suspended in space without support; to the clouds above, which contain the upper waters without bursting, and veil the divine throne, of which the sapphire blue of heaven is the reflection; and then he speaks of the sea lying between Sheôl and heaven, which is confined within fixed bounds, at the extreme boundaries of which light passes over into darkness; - he celebrates all this as proof of the creative might of God. Then he describes the sovereign power of God in the realm of His creation, how He shakes the pillars of heaven, rouses the sea, breaks the monster in pieces, lights up the heavens by chasing away the clouds and piercing the serpent, and thus setting free the sun. But all these - thus he closes - are only meagre outlines of the divine rule, only a faint whisper, which is heard by us as coming from the far distance. Who has the comprehension necessary to take in and speak exhaustively of all the wonders of His infinite nature, which extends throughout the whole creation? From such a profound recognition and so glorious a description of the exaltation of God, the infinite distance between God and man is most clearly proved. Job has adequately shown that his whole soul is full of that which Bildad is anxious to teach him; a soul that only requires a slight impulse to make it overflow with such praise of God, as is not wanting in an universal perception of God, nor is it full of wicked devices. When therefore Bildad maintains against Job that no man is righteous before such an exalted God, Job ought indeed to take it as a warning against such unbecoming utterances concerning God as those which have escaped him; but the universal sinfulness of man is no ground of explanation for his sufferings, for there is a righteousness which avails before God; and of this, job, the suffering servant of God, has a consciousness that cannot be shaken.  <chapter eID="Job.26"/> <div eID="gen8005" type="x-p"/>

These (אלּה retrospective, as in Job 18:21 ) are only קצות, the extremest end-points or outlines of the ways of God, which Job has depicted; the wondrous fulness of His might, which extends through the whole creation, transcends human comprehension; it is only שׁמץ דּבר therefrom that becomes audible to us men. שׁמץ (שׁמץ) is translated by Symm. here ψιθύρισμα, Job 4:12 , ψιτηυρισμός; the Arab. šamiṣa (to speak very quickly, mutter) confirms this idea of the word; Jerome’s translation, vix. parvam stillam sermonis ejus (comp. Job 4:12 , venas , tropical for parts), is doubly erroneous: the rendering of the שׁמץ has the antithesis of רעם against it, and דּבר is not to be understood here otherwise than in ערות דּבר, Deu 23:15 ; Deu 24:1 : shame of something = something that excites a feeling of shame, a whisper of something = some whisper. The notion “somewhat,” which the old expositors attribute to שׁמץ, lies therefore in דבר. מה is exclamatory in a similar manner as in Psa 89:48 : how we hear (נשׁמע, not נשׁמע) only some whisper thereof (בּו partitive, as e.g., Isa 10:22 ), i.e., how little therefrom is audible to us, only as the murmur of a word, not loud and distinct, which reaches us! As in the speech of Bildad the poet makes the opposition of the friends to fade away and cease altogether, as incapable of any further counsel, and hence as conquered, so in Job’s closing speech, which consists of three parts, Job 26:1 , Job 27:1 , Job 29:1 , he shows how Job in every respect, as victor, maintains the field against the friends. The friends have neither been able to loose the knot of Job’s lot of suffering, nor the universal distribution of prosperity and misfortune. Instead of loosing the knot of Job’s lot of suffering, they have cut it, by adding to Job’s heavy affliction the invention of heinous guilt as its ground of explanation; and the knot of the contradictions of human life in general with divine justice they have ignored, in order that they may not be compelled to abandon their dogma, that suffering everywhere necessarily presupposes sin, and sin is everywhere necessarily followed by suffering. Even Job, indeed, is not at present able to solve either one or other of the mysteries; but while the friends’ treatment of these mysteries is untrue, he honours the truth, and keenly perceives that which is mysterious. Then he proves by testimony and an appeal to facts, that the mystery may be acknowledged without therefore being compelled to abandon the fear of God. Job firmly holds to the objective reality and the testimony of his consciousness; in the fear of God he places himself above all those contradictions which are unsolvable by and perplexing to human reason; his faith triumphs over the rationalism of the friends, which is devoid of truth, of justice, and of love. Job first answers Bildad, Job 26:1. He characterizes his poor reply as what it is: as useless, and not pertinent in regard to the questions before them: it is of no service to him, it does not affect him, and is, moreover, a borrowed weapon. For he also is conscious of and can praise God’s exalted and awe-inspiring majesty. He has already shown this twice, Job 9:4-10 ; Job 12:13-25 , and shows here for the third time: its operation is not confined merely to those creatures that immediately surround God in the heavens; it extends, without being restrained by the sea, even down to the lower world; and as it makes the angels above to tremble, so there it sets the shades in consternation. From the lower world, Job’s contemplation rises to the earth, as a body suspended in space without support; to the clouds above, which contain the upper waters without bursting, and veil the divine throne, of which the sapphire blue of heaven is the reflection; and then he speaks of the sea lying between Sheôl and heaven, which is confined within fixed bounds, at the extreme boundaries of which light passes over into darkness; - he celebrates all this as proof of the creative might of God. Then he describes the sovereign power of God in the realm of His creation, how He shakes the pillars of heaven, rouses the sea, breaks the monster in pieces, lights up the heavens by chasing away the clouds and piercing the serpent, and thus setting free the sun. But all these - thus he closes - are only meagre outlines of the divine rule, only a faint whisper, which is heard by us as coming from the far distance. Who has the comprehension necessary to take in and speak exhaustively of all the wonders of His infinite nature, which extends throughout the whole creation? From such a profound recognition and so glorious a description of the exaltation of God, the infinite distance between God and man is most clearly proved. Job has adequately shown that his whole soul is full of that which Bildad is anxious to teach him; a soul that only requires a slight impulse to make it overflow with such praise of God, as is not wanting in an universal perception of God, nor is it full of wicked devices. When therefore Bildad maintains against Job that no man is righteous before such an exalted God, Job ought indeed to take it as a warning against such unbecoming utterances concerning God as those which have escaped him; but the universal sinfulness of man is no ground of explanation for his sufferings, for there is a righteousness which avails before God; and of this, job, the suffering servant of God, has a consciousness that cannot be shaken.
